paragraphs: An American who had spent a long time traveling in Europe once told me, “The English treat their servants with a stiffness and imperiousness of manner which surprise us; but on the other hand the French sometimes treat their attendants with a degree of familiarity or of politeness which we cannot conceive. It looks as if they were afraid to give orders: the posture of the superior and the inferior is ill-maintained.” The remark was just, and I have often made it myself. I have always thought of England as the country where, in our time, the bond of domestic service is drawn tightest, and of France as the country where it is loosest. I have seen masters stand so high, or so low, nowhere else. The Americans fall between these two extremes. That is how the matter looks on the surface. To find the causes behind it, we have to look into it thoroughly.

No society has ever existed in which social conditions were so equal that there were neither rich nor poor, and therefore neither masters nor servants. Democracy does not do away with these two classes, but it alters their dispositions and changes how they relate to each other. Among aristocratic nations, servants form a distinct class, no more varied in makeup than the class of masters. A settled order soon takes shape. In the servants’ class, as in the masters’, a scale develops with many distinctions and clearly marked gradations of rank, and generation follows generation without any change of position. The two communities lie one above the other, always separate, yet governed by similar principles. This aristocratic structure shapes the ideas and customs of servants as powerfully as those of masters; the effects differ, but the same cause is easy to trace. Each class forms a small community within the nation, and in the end fixed ideas of right and wrong arise within it. The various acts of human life are seen in one particular, unchanging light. In the society of servants, as in that of masters, people have great influence over one another: they recognize settled rules, and where there is no law they are guided by a kind of public opinion. Their habits are settled, and their conduct is kept under a certain control.

These men, whose lot is to obey, certainly do not understand fame, virtue, honesty, and honor as their masters do; but they have a pride, a virtue, and an honesty that belong to their condition, and they have an idea, if I may put it so, of a kind of servile honor. *a A class may be mean without all its members being mean-hearted, and to think so would be a great mistake. However lowly the class, the man who stands first in it and has no thought of leaving it holds an aristocratic position, which gives him lofty feelings, pride, and self-respect, and fits him for the higher virtues and for actions above the ordinary. Among aristocratic nations it was by no means rare to find men of noble and vigorous mind in the service of the great, who did not feel the servitude they bore and who submitted to their masters’ will without any fear of displeasing them. But this was hardly ever so among the lower ranks of domestic servants. One may imagine that a man at the bottom of the order of menials stands very low indeed. The French coined a word expressly for the servants of the aristocracy — they called them lackeys. When all other words were used up, “lackey” served as the strongest term for human meanness. Under the old French monarchy, to name a low-spirited, contemptible fellow in a single expression, people would say he had the “soul of a lackey”; the term was enough to convey everything intended. [Footnote a: If one examines closely and in detail the main opinions that guide these men, the analogy appears even more striking, and one is surprised to find among them, just as much as among the haughtiest scions of a feudal line, pride of birth, respect for their ancestors and their descendants, disdain for their inferiors, a dread of contact, and a taste for etiquette, precedents, and antiquity.]

Permanent inequality of conditions not only gives servants certain distinctive virtues and vices; it also puts them in a distinctive relation to their masters. Among aristocratic nations the poor man grows up used to the idea of being commanded: wherever he turns his eyes, he sees the graded structure of society and the look of obedience. In those countries, therefore, the master readily gets prompt, complete, respectful, and easy obedience from his servants, because they revere in him not only their master but the class of masters. He bears down on their will with the entire weight of the aristocracy. He directs their actions — and to some extent even their thoughts. In aristocracies the master often holds an amazing sway, even without realizing it, over the opinions, habits, and customs of those who obey him, and his influence reaches even further than his authority.

In aristocratic communities there are hereditary families of servants as well as of masters, and the same servant families stay attached for several generations to the same master families (like two parallel lines that neither meet nor separate). This considerably changes how the two classes of people relate. So although in aristocratic society master and servant have no natural likeness — although, on the contrary, their fortune, education, and opinions place them at an immense distance on the scale of human beings — time still binds them together in the end. A long chain of shared memories connects them, and however different they are, they come to resemble each other; in democracies, by contrast, where they are naturally almost alike, they always remain strangers. Among an aristocratic people the master comes to regard his servants as an inferior, secondary part of himself, and he often takes an interest in their lot as a last stretch of egotism.

Servants, for their part, are quite willing to see themselves in the same light, and they sometimes identify with the person of the master, so that they become an appendage of him in their own eyes as well as in his. In aristocracies a servant holds a subordinate position he cannot escape; above him stands another man in a superior rank that he cannot lose. On one side are obscurity, poverty, and lifelong obedience; on the other, equally for life, fame, wealth, and command. The two conditions are always distinct and always close together; the tie between them lasts as long as they do. In this predicament the servant ends by detaching his idea of his interest from his own person. He deserts himself, so to speak, or rather he moves himself into his master’s character and so takes on an imaginary personality. He complacently clothes himself in the wealth of those who command him; he shares their fame, raises himself by their rank, and feeds his mind on borrowed greatness, to which he attaches more importance than those who fully and truly possess it. There is something touching, and at the same time ridiculous, in this strange confusion of two different states of being. When these passions of masters pass into the souls of menials, they take on the natural dimensions of the place they now occupy: they shrink and sink lower. What was pride in the master becomes childish vanity and petty ostentation in the servant. The servants of a great man are usually most punctilious about the marks of respect due to him, and they care more about his slightest privileges than he does himself. In France a few of these old servants of the aristocracy can still be met here and there; they have outlived their breed, which will soon vanish altogether with them. In the United States I never saw anyone at all like them. The Americans not only do not know the type; it is hardly possible to make them understand that it ever existed. It is scarcely harder for them to imagine it than for us to form a correct idea of what a slave was among the Romans, or a serf in the Middle Ages. All these men were in fact, though in different degrees, products of the same cause. All of them are withdrawing from our sight and fading into the obscurity of the past, along with the social condition that gave them birth.

Equality of conditions turns servants and masters into new beings and puts them in new positions toward each other. When social conditions are nearly equal, people are constantly changing their situation in life. There is still a class of menials and a class of masters, but these classes are not always made up of the same individuals, still less of the same families, and those who command are no more certain of lasting than those who obey. Because servants do not form a separate people, they have no habits, prejudices, or customs peculiar to themselves; they are not remarkable for any particular turn of mind or mood of feeling. They know no vices or virtues of their condition. They share the education, opinions, feelings, virtues, and vices of their contemporaries, and they are honest men or scoundrels in the same way their masters are. The conditions of servants are no less equal than those of masters. Since no marked ranks or fixed subordination are to be found among them, they will show neither the meanness nor the greatness that marks the aristocracy of menials, as it marks all other aristocracies. I never saw a man in the United States who reminded me of the class of confidential servants of which Europe still keeps a memory, and I never met anything like a lackey: every trace of both has disappeared.

In democracies servants are not only equal among themselves; it may be said that in a certain sense they are the equals of their masters. This needs explaining to be understood correctly. At any moment a servant may become a master, and he aspires to do so; the servant is therefore not a different kind of man from the master. Why, then, does the one have a right to command, and what compels the other to obey? The free and temporary consent of both their wills. Neither is by nature inferior to the other; each becomes so only for a time, by agreement. Within the terms of that agreement, one is a servant and the other a master; beyond it they are two citizens of the commonwealth — two men. I ask the reader particularly to note that servants are not the only ones who see their condition this way; masters regard domestic service in the same light, and the precise limits of authority and obedience are as clearly fixed in the mind of one as in the mind of the other.

When most of the community have long since reached a nearly similar condition, and equality is an old and acknowledged fact, the public mind, which is never swayed by exceptions, sets certain general limits to the value of a man, above or below which no one can long remain. It is in vain that wealth and poverty, authority and obedience, happen to put great distances between two men; public opinion, based on the usual order of things, draws them to a common level and creates a kind of imaginary equality between them, in spite of the real inequality of their conditions. In time this all-powerful opinion penetrates even the hearts of those whose interest might arm them to resist it; it shapes their judgment while it subdues their will. In their inmost convictions the master and the servant no longer see any deep difference between them, and they neither hope nor fear to find one at any time. They are therefore subject neither to disdain nor to anger, and each sees in the other neither humility nor pride. The master holds the contract of service to be the only source of his power, and the servant regards it as the only reason for his obedience. They do not quarrel over their respective positions; each knows his own and keeps to it.

In the French army the common soldier is drawn from nearly the same classes as the officer and may hold the same commissions. Out of the ranks he considers himself entirely equal to his military superiors, and in fact he is; but under arms he does not hesitate to obey, and his obedience is no less prompt, precise, and ready for being voluntary and defined. This example may give an idea of what happens between masters and servants in democratic communities.

It would be absurd to suppose that the warm, deep affections sometimes kindled in the domestic service of an aristocracy will ever spring up between these two men, or that they will show striking instances of self-sacrifice. In aristocracies masters and servants live apart, and often their only dealings are through a third person; yet they commonly stand firmly by one another. In democratic countries master and servant are close together. They are in daily personal contact, but their minds do not mingle; they share occupations, hardly ever interests. Among such a people the servant always thinks of himself as a temporary guest in his masters’ house. He knew nothing of their forefathers, he will see nothing of their descendants, and he has nothing lasting to expect from them. Why then should he entangle his life with theirs, and where would so strange a surrender of himself come from? The relative position of the two men has changed, so their relations must change as well.

I would gladly illustrate all these reflections with the example of the Americans, but for that purpose I must carefully distinguish persons and places. In the South of the Union slavery exists, so everything I have just said is inapplicable there. In the North most servants are either freedmen or the children of freedmen. These people hold a disputed position in public esteem: the laws raise them to the level of their masters, while the customs of the country stubbornly thrust them back down from it. They do not clearly know their own place themselves, and they are almost always either insolent or cringing. But in the Northern States, especially in New England, there are a certain number of whites who agree, for wages, to yield temporary obedience to the will of their fellow citizens. I have heard that these servants usually carry out the duties of their situation punctually and intelligently, and that without thinking themselves naturally inferior to the person who gives them orders, they submit to obeying him without reluctance. They seem to me to bring into service some of the manly habits that independence and equality produce. Having once chosen a hard way of life, they do not try to escape it by indirect means, and they respect themselves enough not to refuse their master the obedience they freely promised. For their part, masters ask nothing of their servants but faithful and strict performance of the agreement: they do not ask for marks of respect, nor claim their love or devoted attachment; it is enough that, as servants, they are exact and honest. It would not be true, then, to say that in democratic society the relation of servants and masters is disorganized. It is organized on another footing; the rule is different, but there is a rule.

It is not my purpose to ask whether the new state of things I have just described is inferior to the one before it, or simply different. It is enough for me that it is fixed and settled, for what matters most to find among men is not any particular ordering, but order. But what shall I say of those sad and troubled times when equality is established amid the tumult of revolution — when democracy, though already introduced into the state of society, still struggles with difficulty against the prejudices and customs of the country? The laws, and in part public opinion, already declare that there is no natural or permanent inferiority between servant and master. But this new belief has not yet reached the master’s innermost convictions, or rather his heart rejects it. In the secret persuasion of his mind, the master thinks he belongs to a peculiar and superior race. He dares not say so, but he shudders as he lets himself be dragged to the same level. His authority over his servants becomes timid and harsh at once. He has already stopped feeling toward them the patronizing kindness that long uncontested power always produces, and he is surprised that, now that he himself has changed, his servant changes too. He wants his attendants to form regular and lasting habits in a condition of domestic service that is only temporary. He demands that they appear content with, and proud of, a servile condition they will one day shake off; that they sacrifice themselves to a man who can neither protect nor ruin them; and, in short, that they enter an indissoluble engagement to a being like themselves, who will last no longer than they will.

Among aristocratic nations it often happens that domestic service does not degrade the character of those who enter it, because they know and imagine no other life, and the amazing inequality between them and their master seems the necessary and unavoidable result of some hidden law of Providence. In democracies domestic service does not degrade the character of those who enter it, because it is freely chosen and taken up for a time only, because public opinion does not stigmatize it, and because it creates no permanent inequality between servant and master. But while the passage from one social condition to another is under way, there is almost always a period when people’s minds waver between the aristocratic idea of subjection and the democratic idea of obedience. Obedience then loses its moral importance in the eyes of the one who obeys. He no longer regards it as a kind of divine obligation, and he does not yet see it in its purely human aspect; it has for him no character of sanctity or justice, and he submits to it as a degrading but profitable condition. At that moment a confused, imperfect phantom of equality haunts the minds of servants. They do not immediately see whether the equality to which they are entitled is to be found inside or outside the bounds of domestic service, and in their hearts they rebel against a subordination to which they have submitted themselves and from which they draw real profit. They consent to serve, and they blush to obey; they like the advantages of service, but not the master; or rather, they are not sure that they should not be masters themselves, and they are inclined to regard the one who gives them orders as an unjust usurper of their own rights. That is when the home of every citizen presents a spectacle somewhat like the gloomy look of political society. A secret internal war goes on there between powers that are always rivals and always suspicious of one another. The master is ill-natured and weak, the servant ill-natured and intractable; the one constantly tries to evade, by unfair restrictions, his obligation to protect and to pay, the other his obligation to obey. The reins of domestic government dangle between them, to be snatched by one or the other. The lines dividing authority from oppression, liberty from license, and right from might are so jumbled and blurred in their eyes that no one knows exactly what he is, what he may be, or what he ought to be. Such a condition is not democracy, but revolution.
